kw: Declaration of the Rights of Man
lede: A teenage French marquis who slipped past his own king's orders to fight for American liberty, became George Washington's beloved protege, tried to steer France's revolution to a moderate end, and spent five years in Austrian prisons for it.

ps: Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, was born on 6 September 1757 at the castle of Chavaniac in Auvergne, in central France. Orphaned young, he was one of the richest nobles in the country by his teens.

At 19 he sailed to America, served as a general in the Revolutionary War and helped trap the British army at Yorktown in 1781. Back home he drafted a first version of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and commanded the National Guard of Paris in 1789.

The Revolution turned against him, and from 1792 to 1797 he was a prisoner in Prussia and Austria. He remained a voice for liberal government for the rest of his life, and died in Paris on 20 May 1834, aged 76.

His father, a colonel, was killed by a British cannonball at the Battle of Minden in 1759, before Gilbert turned two. He was raised by his grandmother and aunts in Chavaniac, reading tales of Roman heroes. By his own account he once went out hoping to hunt down a wolf that was killing local livestock.
His mother and grandfather died in 1770, leaving him, at twelve, a huge fortune. He was sent to school in Paris and trained for the army.
In 1774, aged 16, he married Adrienne de Noailles, 14, from one of the most powerful families at court. The match was arranged, but it grew into a devoted marriage.

ps.t: 1775 to 1777. At a dinner in Metz he heard about the American revolt and, he later wrote, his heart was enlisted at once. He signed on with the American agent Silas Deane as a major general.
ps.why: The Metz dinner story comes from his own memoirs, written decades later. His agreement with Deane survives.

ps: 1777. Louis XVI forbade him to go. He bought his own ship, La Victoire, sailed from Spain in April and landed in South Carolina in June. Congress made him an unpaid major general. He met Washington in August and was shot in the leg at the Battle of Brandywine in September.

1778 to 1781. He shared the winter at Valley Forge, went home in 1779 to press for French troops and money, and returned in 1780 ahead of a French army. In 1781 he led American forces in Virginia, shadowing the British general Cornwallis until French and American armies closed the trap at Yorktown in October.

Paris, July 1789. Elected to the Estates General, he presented a draft declaration of rights on 11 July, written with advice from Thomas Jefferson. Days after the fall of the Bastille he was named commander of the new National Guard.
Versailles, October 1789. When a crowd marched on the palace, he protected the royal family and escorted them to Paris. For a while he was the most popular man in France.
Champ de Mars, July 1791. His National Guard fired on a crowd petitioning to remove the king, killing dozens. Radicals never forgave him.

1792 to 1797. After the monarchy fell in August 1792 he was declared a traitor and fled to the Austrian Netherlands, where enemy troops arrested him. He was held in Prussian and then Austrian fortresses, last at Olmutz, in today's Czech Republic. Napoleon's victories won his release in 1797.

1824 to 1825. At President Monroe's invitation he toured all 24 states, greeted by huge crowds. In 1830 he again commanded the National Guard during the July Revolution and helped make Louis-Philippe king.

The draft Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789). Much of it was reworked by the Assembly, but the final text shared his belief in natural rights, equality before the law and power coming from the nation.

ps.t: The tricolour cockade. In July 1789 he is credited with joining the white of the monarchy to the red and blue of Paris, the origin of the French flag.
ps.why: He claimed the idea himself, and it is widely accepted, but others were involved.

ps: Abolition. He urged Washington to free enslaved people and in 1785 bought a plantation in French Guiana to try a gradual freeing of the workers there. He joined the French antislavery Society of the Friends of the Blacks.
Religious freedom. He campaigned for civil rights for French Protestants, granted in 1787.
Constitutional monarchy. Throughout his life he wanted kings bound by law and elected assemblies, which left him too radical for royalists and too moderate for revolutionaries.
George Washington (1732 to 1799), his commander and hero. Lafayette named his son George Washington Lafayette, and Washington treated him like a son.

Adrienne de Lafayette (1759 to 1807). Imprisoned in Paris during the Terror, she lost her grandmother, mother and sister to the guillotine in 1794. On release she took their two daughters to share his cell at Olmutz.
Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826), US minister in Paris in 1789, who advised him on the declaration of rights.
John Adams (1735 to 1826), whom he knew in the revolution and in Paris, and visited at Quincy in 1824.
Alexander Hamilton (1755 or 1757 to 1804), his fellow aide and friend on Washington's staff.
Napoleon Bonaparte (1769 to 1821), who freed him but whose one-man rule he opposed.
He was born a courtier of Louis XV, a world of powdered wigs and inherited privilege, and lived to see two revolutions, Napoleon's empire and two returns of the Bourbon kings.
For young French nobles of the 1770s, the American cause was also a chance to strike back at Britain, which had beaten France in the Seven Years' War.
Ideas of the Enlightenment, about rights, reason and consent of the governed, moved across the Atlantic in both directions, and he carried them in person.
Americans called him the Hero of Two Worlds. Dozens of towns and counties, Lafayette Square in Washington and Lafayette College in Pennsylvania are named after him.
He was buried in Picpus Cemetery in Paris, beside Adrienne, under soil he had brought back from Bunker Hill. An American flag flies over the grave.
In 2002 the United States made him an honorary citizen, one of only a handful of people given that honour.

myths.c: He defied his king to sail to America.
myths.t: Louis XVI and his own family forbade it, and an order was issued to stop him. He bought a ship with his own money and went anyway.
Washington had no legal tie to him. Their bond was close and fatherly, and Lafayette signed letters as a devoted son, but there was no adoption.

myths.c: He escaped the guillotine by a whisker.
myths.t: He fled in August 1792, before the Terror began, and spent it in foreign prisons. His wife's family were not so lucky.

myths.c: General Pershing said 'Lafayette, we are here' in 1917.
myths.t: The words were spoken at Lafayette's grave on 4 July 1917 by Colonel Charles Stanton, one of Pershing's officers. Pershing himself later credited Stanton.
